title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 301
paragraphs: In this occupation certain persons employ themselves regularly, and inherit this as a craft. Whenever a corpse is conveyed to them, they show those who have brought it wooden models of corpses made lifelike by painting, and the best of the ways of embalming they say is that of him whose name I think it impiety to mention when speaking of such a matter. The second that they show is less good than this, and also less expensive; and the third is the cheapest of all. Having told them this, they ask in which way they wish the corpse of their friend to be prepared. Then, after they have agreed for a certain price, the relatives depart, and the others, left behind in the buildings, embalm according to the best of these ways as follows. First, with a crooked iron tool they draw out the brain through the nostrils, extracting it partly thus and partly by pouring in drugs; after this with a sharp Ethiopian stone they make a cut along the side and take out the whole contents of the belly, and when they have cleaned out the cavity and rinsed it with palm-wine, they cleanse it again with pounded spices. Then they fill the belly with pure myrrh pounded up, cassia, and other spices (except frankincense), and sew it together again. Having so done, they keep it for embalming covered up in natron for seventy days, but for a longer time than this it is not permitted to embalm. When the seventy days are past, they wash the corpse and wrap the whole body in fine linen cut into bands, smearing these beneath with gum, which the Egyptians use generally in place of glue. Then the kinsfolk receive the corpse from them and have a wooden figure made in the shape of a man; and when they have had this made, they enclose the corpse within it, and having shut it up, they then store it in a sepulchral chamber, setting it to stand upright against the wall.
